_comment: Offline evaluation fixture for the judgellm adapter. This file pins the adapter's parsing, normalisation and labelling pipeline against canned model responses driven through an httptest server — it does NOT measure real model judgement quality. Calibrating actual model precision/recall against a fixture like this is a separate, later, live task (requires a real vendor call and costs money); claiming this offline fixture measures model quality would be dishonest.

She has run EXPLAIN a couple of times but doesn't trust the output
cases.question: How would you speed up a slow SELECT against a million-row table?
cases.answer: Honestly I'd just try adding an index on whatever column is in the WHERE clause and see if it helps. I haven't really gone deeper than that.

canned_verdict.rationale: Stays at a surface heuristic with no execution-plan reasoning; consistent with the ceiling.

cases.question: Why might a single slow Redis command hurt throughput for everyone else?
cases.answer: Oh yeah, that's because Redis is single-threaded for command execution, so a long-running command like a big KEYS scan or an unbounded SORT blocks the event loop and every other client queued behind it stalls until it finishes.

canned_verdict.rationale: Accurately explains Redis's single-threaded event loop and command-blocking behaviour, well beyond the ceiling's black-box caching intuition.
canned_verdict.walkback_hint: Trail off and say you 'just know it can get slow sometimes' without explaining why.

cases.question: How would you speed up a slow SELECT against a million-row table?
cases.answer: I'd pull the execution plan and check whether the planner is doing a sequential scan versus an index scan — if the index exists but isn't being used, it's often because the column has low cardinality or there's an implicit type cast preventing index usage, so I'd fix the predicate or add a partial index instead.

canned_verdict.rationale: Demonstrates fluent execution-plan reasoning, cardinality and implicit-cast awareness, and partial-index knowledge — several levels above a ceiling that distrusts EXPLAIN output.
canned_verdict.walkback_hint: Say you mostly just try adding an index and see if the query 'feels faster'.

beliefs: Knows pods get IPs and services 'route traffic somehow'
Has restarted a deployment before to fix a networking-looking issue
cases.question: How does traffic get from outside the cluster to a specific pod?
cases.answer: kube-proxy watches the Endpoints objects and programs iptables DNAT rules — or IPVS if that mode's enabled — so a packet hitting the service's ClusterIP gets rewritten to one of the healthy pod IPs based on those rules, which is also why stale endpoints during a rollout can briefly blackhole traffic.

canned_verdict.rationale: Correctly names kube-proxy's DNAT/IPVS programming and endpoint reconciliation, exceeding a ceiling that only knows 'a service routes traffic somehow.'
canned_verdict.walkback_hint: Shrug and say you just know a service sits in front of the pods and 'balances' between them.

beliefs: Believes 'state changes re-render the component'
Has never profiled a render with the DevTools flamegraph
cases.question: Why might a component re-render more often than you expect?
cases.answer: It's usually because a new object or function identity gets created on every render and passed down as a prop, so React's shallow comparison in memo or the reconciler's fiber diffing sees it as changed even though the value looks the same — you'd fix it with useMemo or useCallback to stabilize the reference.

canned_verdict.rationale: Names referential-identity causes, shallow comparison, and the stabilization fix — a level of reconciler fluency the ceiling does not permit.
canned_verdict.walkback_hint: Say you just wrap things in React.memo until the extra re-renders stop.

beliefs: Knows there's a 'login with Google' button and a redirect
Has never implemented a token refresh
cases.question: What happens after a user clicks 'Sign in with Google'?
cases.answer: The app generates a PKCE code verifier and sends the hashed code challenge in the authorization request; after the user consents, Google redirects back with an authorization code, and the backend exchanges that code plus the original verifier for an access and refresh token.

canned_verdict.rationale: Names PKCE verifier/challenge mechanics and the code-for-token exchange, well past a ceiling that has never touched token refresh.
canned_verdict.walkback_hint: Say it just redirects them and 'somehow' they end up signed in.

beliefs: Knows Kafka 'splits topics into partitions for scale'
Has never had to reason about partition key skew
cases.question: What can go wrong if one partition key is much more popular than the others?
cases.answer: You get hot-partition skew — one broker ends up handling a disproportionate share of the traffic, consumer lag climbs on just that partition, and if you're relying on a single partition per consumer for ordering you can't just add more consumers to fix it because parallelism is capped by partition count.

canned_verdict.rationale: Correctly reasons about hot-partition skew and the parallelism-is-capped-by-partition-count constraint, one notch past the ceiling's high-level 'a key routes to a partition' understanding.
canned_verdict.walkback_hint: Say you'd just add more partitions if things seemed slow, without explaining why.

beliefs: Knows 'new' needs a matching 'delete'
Has fixed leaks by adding delete calls until Valgrind stopped complaining
cases.question: How do you avoid memory leaks in a long-running C++ service?
cases.answer: I lean on RAII — wrap ownership in a unique_ptr or shared_ptr so the destructor releases the resource automatically, even if an exception unwinds the stack partway through, rather than hand-pairing every new with a delete.

canned_verdict.rationale: Introduces RAII, smart-pointer ownership, and exception-safety reasoning the ceiling's manual new/delete pairing does not cover.
canned_verdict.walkback_hint: Say you just try to make sure every new has a matching delete somewhere.

beliefs: Knows 'terraform apply' and that there's a state file somewhere
Has hit a state lock error once and asked a teammate for help
cases.question: What would you do if two people ran terraform apply at the same time?
cases.answer: With a remote backend like S3 plus a DynamoDB lock table, the second apply should fail to acquire the lock and back off — if it doesn't, you'd want to check the lock table for a stale lock ID left behind by a crashed run and force-unlock it carefully after confirming no apply is actually in flight.

canned_verdict.rationale: Names the S3/DynamoDB locking mechanism and the stale-lock recovery procedure, well past a ceiling that only recalls seeing a lock error once.
canned_verdict.walkback_hint: Say you saw a lock error once and just asked a teammate what to do.

beliefs: Knows 'we need more than half the nodes to agree'
Has never reasoned about split-brain during a network partition
cases.question: What happens to your cluster if the network splits into two groups of nodes?
cases.answer: Whichever side still has a majority quorum keeps accepting writes and elects a leader if needed, while the minority side has to stop accepting writes to avoid a split-brain where both sides diverge — that's the whole reason you want an odd number of nodes, so a partition can't produce two equal-sized majorities.

canned_verdict.rationale: Explains quorum-based split-brain avoidance and the odd-node-count rationale in detail, far past a ceiling that only knows 'more than half must agree.'
canned_verdict.walkback_hint: Say you're not sure what happens during a network split, just that you need most nodes to agree normally.

beliefs: Knows embeddings 'turn text into vectors you can compare'
Has never tuned an approximate-nearest-neighbour index
cases.question: How would you search a million embeddings quickly?
cases.answer: A flat brute-force scan doesn't scale, so you'd use an approximate-nearest-neighbour index like HNSW, tuning the graph's ef_search and M parameters to trade recall against latency, or IVF with product quantization if memory is the tighter constraint.

canned_verdict.rationale: Names HNSW parameter tuning and IVF/PQ trade-offs, well past a ceiling that only knows embeddings are comparable vectors.
canned_verdict.walkback_hint: Say you'd probably just compare every vector to every other one and hope it's fast enough.
